opus-5.5.text:
I really think of AlphaFold as a complement to experiment, not a replacement for it. The way I like to put it is that AlphaFold is extraordinarily good at giving you a hypothesis, very quickly and very cheaply, and experiments are how you find out what's actually true in the specific system you care about.

Before AlphaFold, a lot of biologists would wait months or years for a structure, and sometimes they'd never get one at all. Now they can have a confident prediction in minutes, and that changes what experiments they choose to do. Instead of spending two years trying to crystallize a protein just to learn its rough shape, they can start from a predicted model and go straight to the interesting questions: which residues matter for function, where a drug might bind, what a mutation is likely to disrupt. The prediction makes the experiment smarter.

It's also become a tool inside experimental structural biology itself. People use predicted models for molecular replacement in crystallography, to fit into cryo-EM maps that are too low resolution to build from scratch, or to interpret cross-linking and other sparse data. So the boundary between "computational" and "experimental" has gotten a lot blurrier, in a good way.

But I'm always careful to stress the limits. AlphaFold learned from the Protein Data Bank, which is decades of painstaking experimental work. It doesn't exist without experiment. And it predicts largely a static structure. It can tell you a lot, but it doesn't directly tell you about dynamics, about how a protein moves between conformations, about the effects of the cellular environment, or about every detail of how proteins interact with ligands and partners. The confidence measures help here. We put a lot of effort into making the model tell you when it doesn't know, and I'd encourage people to take those seriously.

So my hope is that AlphaFold shifts where experimental effort goes. Less effort on the parts we can now predict well, more on the parts that are genuinely hard and genuinely new: dynamics, complexes, function, the things that tell us how biology actually works. If it does that, then it's done its job.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that AlphaFold is a complement to experimental structural biology, not a replacement for it, and I'd push back on anyone who frames it as the end of crystallography or cryo-EM.

What AlphaFold really does is change where the experimental effort goes. Before, if you wanted to understand a protein, you might spend a year or two just getting a structure, and that structure was often the whole paper. Now you can get a very good hypothesis in a few minutes, and the interesting question becomes what to do with it. So experimentalists are spending less time on the "what does this fold look like" question and more time on the things a prediction can't tell you: dynamics, conformational changes, what happens when a ligand binds, how a complex actually assembles in a cell, what the post-translational modifications are doing. Those are harder questions, and frankly they're more interesting ones.

There's also a very practical loop. A lot of cryo-EM and crystallography groups now use AlphaFold models to solve the phase problem or to fit into low-resolution density. So the predictions are literally inside the experimental pipeline. And it goes the other way too: every new structure deposited in the PDB is training data for the next generation of models. The field only works because experimentalists spent fifty years building that database, and the models are only as good as that foundation.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that AlphaFold tells you where it's uncertain. The confidence metrics are, in some ways, as important as the coordinates. If the model says it's unsure about a region, that's a flag that something interesting may be happening there, maybe disorder, maybe a region that only orders on binding, and that's exactly where an experiment is worth doing. So I think of it less as "prediction versus experiment" and more as prediction telling you which experiment to run.

Where I'd be careful is with people treating a predicted structure as ground truth. It's a very good hypothesis. It's not a measurement. The things that are genuinely new, novel folds, unusual complexes, proteins far from anything in the training distribution, those still need experimental validation, and I think that's going to stay true for a long time.

astra-6.text:
I see AlphaFold as complementary to experiments. It gives you a structural hypothesis that can help you decide what to measure, which mutations to make, or how to interpret data you already have. That can make the experimental process much more focused.

But a structure isn’t the whole story of a protein. You want to understand how it moves, what it interacts with, and how its behavior changes in different conditions. And you have to distinguish the parts of a prediction you can trust from those where there’s substantial uncertainty.

So the exciting thing is the interaction between prediction and experiment: you make a prediction, test what it implies, and use the results to build a better understanding of the biology.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of AlphaFold as complementary to experiments. It gives you a structural hypothesis that can help you decide what experiment to do next, or help interpret the data you already have. If you're working with cryo-EM or crystallography, for example, a predicted structure can be a useful starting point.

But a structure isn't the whole story of a protein. You still want to know how it moves, what it interacts with, and how its behavior changes under different conditions. And you have to pay attention to where the prediction is confident and where it isn't. The exciting thing is the feedback loop: experiments give us the foundation for making predictions, and predictions can help experimentalists ask more precise questions.
